task: Write one sentence of your own using the word brusque. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know brusque should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The concierge answered every question with a brusque wave toward the elevators, and guests wondered what they had done to offend him.
Direct is milder than brusque: a direct answer skips the padding but keeps its manners.
Surly is harsher than brusque — brusque is short with you; surly is short with you and hostile about it.

Gruff is roughness of voice and manner — a low bark that can hide a kind heart underneath. Brusque is about brevity, not sound: a brusque reply is short to the point of rudeness, however warm or smooth the voice that delivers it.

Offhand means tossed out casually, without ceremony or much thought — an offhand remark can even be friendly. Brusque has a sting the casualness lacks: a brusque answer is short in a way that dismisses you, and it lands as rude.
taking time to be polite
friendly and welcoming in manner

Brusque came to English whole, via French from Italian brusco, 'sharp, tart' — a wine word turned manner word. Its Latin source, the name of a prickly shrub, produced no other common English word, so brusque stands alone.
Brusque means short, abrupt, dismissive.

Reviews of the mountain guesthouse agreed on two points: the views were glorious and the owner was brusque — questions at breakfast got one-syllable answers, and requests for extra towels got the towels, flung, with no reply at all.
Brusque describes the surface of someone's manner — short, abrupt, dismissive — not what drives it.
That keeps it milder than surly, which carries real hostility: a brusque host has run out of words; a surly one wants you gone.
Use brusque for a manner that is short to the point of rudeness — service-counter shortness, not open hostility.
Its unit neighbor curt does the same work for a single reply (a curt nod, a curt 'No'); brusque more often paints the whole manner.
When the shortness turns hostile, you have left brusque behind for surly.

The line outside Sho's noodle counter starts forming at eleven, though Sho has never once said 'welcome' to anyone in it.
Orders are taken in four words or fewer.
Questions about the menu get 'Read the board.' Requests for substitutions get 'No.' Then the noodles arrive, and they are perfect.
A food blogger once described the service as brusque to the point of comedy — every answer clipped short, every pleasantry skipped, and nothing about it warm.
Regulars insist there is no anger in it.
Sho simply refuses to spend words he could spend on broth; the shortness is pace, not spite.
The blogger's verdict stood anyway: you come for the bowl, and you learn not to ask follow-up questions.
